newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - American Brands CEO eyes takeovers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - American Brands CEO eyes takeovers.

text.p: American Brands Inc, following the spinoff of its U.K-based Gallaher tobacco operations, will emerge a streamlined yet diverse company with plenty of room for further acquisitions, Chairman Thomas Hays said Tuesday.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, Hays said the company planned to continue its acquisition program, which scored a stunning success with its purchase last year of Cobra Golf.
At the same time, the split does much to remove tobacco from the company's identity on Wall Street.
"We are cautious and considered, but we do plan to continue an active acquisition program, and we'll have the resources to do it," Hays said.

American Brands, with $4.6 billion in sales for the 12 months ended in June, will change its name to Fortune Brands when the spinoff is complete in six to 10 months. It already has some of the most recognizable consumer products brands.

Besides Cobra golf clubs, its golf line includes Titleist golf balls and Foot-Joy golf shoes. Master Lock padlocks, Moen faucets, DeKuyper and Jim Beam liquors and Day-Timer calendars all rest at or near the top of their markets.
"Whether we would make another acquisition in the short term in golf -- we'd certainly be willing to. It's a great business.
"But we are very well positioned in golf, so we're looking at office products and hardware, and in distilled spirits also. We intend to support all of our companies," Hays said.
Wall Street cheered the move, pumping the shares up to a new 52-week high of 49-1/8 before paring gains back to 48, up 3-1/2, at midday.
Hays said he suspected the company's announced intention of buying back up to 10 million shares contributed to the advance.

But analysts said -- and Hays acknowledged -- that the perception among investors was that the stigma of tobacco had been more thoroughly removed, even though American Brands rid itself of litigation risk in the United States when it sold its American Tobacco Co unit in 1994 to B.A.T Industries Plc's Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp.
"I think it's part of the benefit, certainly. There was some ongoing confusion: Were we still in the domestic tobacco business?" Hays said.
UBS Securities analyst Anton Brenner said, "I don't think there's any qustion but that the presence of the tobacco business hurt the valuation (of American Brands stock). This will remove that."
"Also, its tobacco business was not growing, or at least wasn't going to grow at a rapid rate. The U.K is a very mature cigarette market," Brenner said.
For Gallaher, the spinoff allows it to be a tobacco company -- just a tobacco company, and not beholden to the strategies of a conglomerate, Hays said.

Gallaher's 39-percent market share tops Britain, with Benson & Hedges and Silk Cut premium brands. Sales in 1995 were 4.08 billion sterling, up from four billion in 1994 and an increase of 13 percent from 1992's 3.61 billion sterling.

"When American Brands, as a holding company, weighed investment opportunities for Gallaher compared to investment opportunities for our other operations, there had to be a balance," Hays said. "Now they will have a complete and total dedication to tobacco operations."
"There's a lot of good news today. I looked up 'fortune' in the dictionary, and it means a lot of money. We have very high hopes for Fortune Brands," Hays said.
